lead: A theodolite reads two angles at once: one horizontal, one vertical. It can do that only if three axes inside it stay square to each other. Those axes cannot be machined perfect and they drift with jolts and temperature, so the instrument carries screws and bubbles to restore the geometry. Temporary adjustments are made at every station and take a few minutes. Permanent adjustments are made rarely, by a trained hand, and only when a field test fails.
prereq: You need: measurement of lengths and angles, and the least count of a vernier, from Unit 1, Measurements, errors, accuracy and precision.

blocks.text: A theodolite measures a horizontal angle between two directions and a vertical angle above or below the horizon. It does this with two graduated circles. The horizontal circle lies in a horizontal plane and is read through verniers. The vertical circle turns with the telescope and gives the elevation.

The instrument is built around three axes. The vertical axis is the spindle inside the tribrach; levelling makes it truly vertical, along gravity. The horizontal axis, also called the trunnion axis, carries the telescope, so the telescope swings up and down about it. The line of collimation is the straight line from the centre of the objective through the crossing point of the cross hairs to the target.

Adjustment means restoring three right angles and two settings that go with them: the line of collimation square to the horizontal axis, the horizontal axis square to the vertical axis, and the plate level axis square to the vertical axis, with the altitude level parallel to the line of collimation and the vertical-circle index at zero. When all hold, a vertical angle means what it claims.

Face left is the position with the vertical circle on the observer's left when the telescope points forward. Face right is the reverse. Transiting is turning the telescope end for end about the horizontal axis, through 180°. Changing face means transiting and then swinging the upper part 180° about the vertical axis until the same target is sighted again; the vertical circle is now on the other side. A swing alone does not change face. On a correct instrument, face left and face right readings of the same target differ by exactly 180°.

sections.h3: Parts and what each one does

blocks.text: The moving parts sit on two concentric spindles. The inner spindle carries the upper plate and the telescope; the outer spindle carries the lower plate and the horizontal circle, and is fixed to the tribrach.

head: Part
Job
rows: Telescope, focusing screw
Magnifies the target; the screw moves the objective (external focus) or an internal focusing lens so the image falls on the cross hairs
Diaphragm and cross hairs
Sighting reference; the centre of the hairs fixes the line of collimation
Vertical circle
Graduated arc turning with the telescope; read for vertical angles
Horizontal circle, verniers A and B
Graduated ring in the horizontal plane; two verniers cancel eccentricity
Upper and lower plates
Upper carries the verniers; lower carries the circle
Inner and outer spindles
Concentric axes joining the plates to the tribrach
Foot screws (three)
Tilt the tribrach until the vertical axis is truly vertical
Plate levels (two)
Bubbles at right angles; show when the vertical axis is vertical
Altitude (telescope) level
Bubble on the telescope; sets the vertical-circle index
Clamps and tangent screws
Clamp locks a plate; tangent screw gives slow motion for the final setting
Optical plummet
Sights the station mark down the vertical axis

blocks.text: The upper clamp locks the upper plate to the lower plate, and its tangent screw then turns it by a hair. The lower clamp locks the lower plate to the tribrach.
LC = (value of one main-scale division) ÷ (number of vernier divisions)
blocks.where: LC is the least count, the smallest angle the vernier can read. On a common 20″ theodolite the horizontal circle is graduated to 20′ and the vernier has 60 divisions, so LC = 20′ ÷ 60 = 1200″ ÷ 60 = 20″. One minute is 60 seconds of arc.

blocks.text: Temporary adjustment is done at every setup. It makes the vertical axis vertical, puts the instrument over the mark and removes parallax. Nothing is corrected permanently.

items: Stand the tripod over the station mark, legs firm and about shoulder width, head roughly level.
Look through the optical plummet and slide the instrument on the tribrach head until the mark sits under the cross.
Centre the plate level bubble with two foot screws, turning both thumbs towards each other or both away from each other, choosing the direction that moves the bubble to the centre.
Turn the instrument through 90° and centre the bubble with the third foot screw. Repeat in the first position until the bubble stays central all round.
Focus the eyepiece on the cross hairs against a bright sky until the hairs are sharp.
Sight the target and turn the focusing screw until the image is sharp.
Move your eye up and down behind the eyepiece. If the image slides over the hairs, there is parallax; refocus until it stops.

blocks.text: Check setting over again after levelling; the two disturb each other slightly. On sloping ground keep one leg downhill. Centre the bubble with the foot screws only, never by shifting the legs.

sections.h3: Permanent adjustment: six tests, six corrections

blocks.text: Permanent adjustment is done rarely and in a fixed order: plate level, diaphragm, telescope level, collimation, spindle, vertical-circle index. Each test assumes the ones before it hold, so a fault left in the first test spoils every test after it.

head: Test
What it checks
Correction
rows: Plate level test
Plate level axis square to vertical axis
If transiting leaves the bubble 2n divisions off, bring it back n with the level's capstan screws, re-level and repeat
Diaphragm test
Vertical hair truly vertical (perpendicular to the horizontal axis)
Rotate the diaphragm until the hair follows a fixed point during a slow swing
Telescope level test
Telescope bubble axis parallel to line of collimation
Adjust the bubble with its capstan screws
Collimation test
Line of collimation square to horizontal axis
Move the vertical hair by the diaphragm screws through half the face-left minus face-right difference
Spindle test
Horizontal axis square to vertical axis
Workshop job: the trunnion bearing is shimmed or reamed, not screwed
Vertical-circle index
Reading zero on a horizontal sight with the altitude bubble centred
Reset the index or the vernier to zero

blocks.text: The plate level test runs by transiting. If the bubble wanders, the level axis and the vertical axis are not square, and the drift is twice the error. The collimation test compares face left and face right on a distant, well-defined point; the mean is free of the error, so field work on a suspect instrument is booked on both faces.

figure.caption: The line of collimation must be square to the horizontal axis, and the horizontal axis square to the vertical axis; the foot screws make the bottom bar truly vertical.

items.label: Horizontal axis

items.label: Vertical axis
items.note: made truly vertical by foot screws

spec.aria: Three stacked bars: line of collimation on the horizontal axis, horizontal axis on the vertical axis, each needing to be square to the one below.

examples.question: A 20″ vernier theodolite is levelled on a station and the plate level bubble is centred. The telescope is transited 180° about the horizontal axis and the bubble stands 4 divisions off centre. One division is 30″. (i) Find the error between the plate level axis and the vertical axis. (ii) State the correction.
steps: Transiting reverses the level relative to the vertical axis, so the bubble shows twice the axis error.
Correction: bring the bubble back 2 divisions (60″) with the capstan screws of the plate level. This tilts the level tube, not the instrument.
Re-level with the foot screws, transit again, and repeat until the bubble stays centred in both positions.
examples.answer: The plate level axis is out of square by 60″ (2 divisions); bring the bubble back 2 divisions with the plate level capstan screws, re-level and repeat until it stays centred.
examples.check:
div = 4
sens = 30
err_div = div / 2
err_sec = err_div * sens
print(err_div)
print(err_sec)

traps: Correcting the whole bubble drift. Transiting shows twice the axis error, so 4 divisions off means a 2-division error.
Mixing temporary and permanent adjustment. Temporary is every setup; permanent is rare and follows a failing test.

Confusing transiting with changing face. Transiting turns the telescope end for end about the horizontal axis; changing face is transiting plus swinging the upper part 180° to re-sight the target on the other face.
Expecting one test to reveal everything. Each test checks one axis relation, in order.
Unit slips: 20″ is twenty seconds of arc, not minutes or millimetres, and 1′ = 60″.

quiz.q: What is the line of collimation?
quiz.a: The straight line from the centre of the objective through the intersection of the cross hairs to the target.
Turning the telescope end for end about the horizontal axis through 180°, so objective and eyepiece swap ends.

quiz.q: Why does the horizontal circle carry two verniers, A and B?
quiz.a: They read opposite ends of a diameter. If the circle centre does not coincide with the spindle axis, one reads high and the other equally low, so the mean cancels the eccentricity error.

quiz.q: The plate level bubble stands 3 divisions off centre after transiting. One division is 25″. Find the axis error and the correction.
quiz.a: Drift = 3 × 25″ = 75″. Axis error = 75″ ÷ 2 = 37.5″ = 1.5 divisions. Bring the bubble back 1.5 divisions with the capstan screws, re-level, transit and repeat.

quiz.q: A collimation test on a distant point gives face left 12°24′00″ and face right 192°24′40″. Find the collimation error.
quiz.a: 192°24′40″ − 180° = 12°24′40″. The faces differ by 40″, so collimation error = 40″ ÷ 2 = 20″. The correct direction is the mean, 12°24′20″.

quiz.q: The spindle test fails on a site instrument. Why is it not corrected in the field?
quiz.a: The horizontal axis must be made square to the vertical axis, which means altering the trunnion bearings or standards, factory-aligned parts. A field screw would only tilt the telescope and add a new error. Send it to the workshop and observe on both faces meanwhile.

quiz.q: Why must the eyepiece be focused before the objective?
quiz.a: The eyepiece first brings the cross hairs to the plane a relaxed eye sees sharply. The objective then brings the target image into that same plane, so both are sharp together and parallax disappears.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern theodolites use absolute encoders instead of glass circles and electronic levels instead of bubbles, but the three-axis geometry is unchanged; a dual-axis compensator measures residual tilt and subtracts it. A total station adds EDM and a processor to the same frame.
